newsitem.title: UK: Weather produces mixed outlook for N.Europe beet.
newsitem.headline: Weather produces mixed outlook for N.Europe beet.

text.p: Northern Europe experienced mixed weather conditions across its sugar beet growing areas during September, leading to differing crop prospects for the region's key growers, industry sources and beet analysts said on Tuesday.

Beet planters in France, the largest producer in the European Union (EU), said the results of the fifth and last field test suggested the dry weather and cool temperatures seen over the month were hampering crop recovery.
An analyst for the national beet planters federation (CGB) said the adverse weather conditions had limited root growth but helped boost sugar content.
"It is now quite obvious that the beets will not make up ground lost earlier in the season," he said.
Beets in Normandy, Alsace and the Loiret areas have seen the best performance while crops in the Yonne and Oise regions suffered most from a prolonged drought in the spring.
The results of the first four tests by planters were broadly in line with the four tests carried out by producers. Both producers and planters traditionally conduct tests in parallel.
While planters are now forecasting final yields at 9.5 tonnes white value after 9.8 tonnes in 1995/96, the FIRS sugar intervention board is assuming 9.4 tonnes after 9.8 tonnes.
Beet harvesting got under way last week in France, around the same time as in 1995.
As France's total sowing area is lower than last year, there will be fewer beets to process so refineries may stop operations three to four days earlier than originally scheduled.
But the weather told a different story in Germany, the EU's second largest beet producer, and also elsewhere in the region.

The WVZ sugar industry association released the results of its fifth beet test on Monday, confirming the trend of recovery seen in recent weeks. Yields, sugar contents and weights were all higher than the equivalent test in 1995.
A WVZ official in Bonn said the beet harvest, which runs to the end of November, was producing "satisfactory results".
"Official crop forecasts have not been revised but may well be raised if the campaign continues to run that well," he said.
Farmers have reported good beet growth and sugar content on moist soils after recent rainy spells, which hampered grain harvesting and delayed winter sowings of other crops.
But cloudy weather and occasional rain is forecast for much of this week and while wet weather is ideal for beets, the weather may be slightly too cold for the plants to prosper.
"Wet and warm weather would allow for optimal sugar development," said a farm union source in Lower Saxony, a key beet region.
In Britain, the timely September rains have produced a dramatic improvement in crop quality and beet experts said higher yields could prompt an upward revision of sugar output.
Rainfall on areas with lighter soils in August reduced the drought stress earlier in the campaign and the relatively mild September weather caused an unexpectedly high growth rate.
"It's the most growth they've ever seen in September, which is unusual, but some mild conditions are helping that along," said an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU).
"If things carry on this way, British Sugar may revise upwards their estimates on sugar production," she said.
But a British Sugar spokesman declined to comment on output potential or on numbers of beets sown per hectare, but said the crop was continuing on course for an average result.
The improved outlook for the crop has resulted in farmers requesting factories to open slightly earlier than scheduled.
But rains are still needed to moisten areas with hard ground, although beets in some key areas are ready for processing despite suffering from an earlier drought.
As Britain's mild climate allows for a longer harvest, beet lifting can continue as late as December because there is not as much danger of damaging cold as in some other European nations.
Recent weather conditions in the Netherlands are also reported to have benefited the beet crop.
Alfons Calon, agricultural affairs director at Suiker Unie, the country's largest grower, said the weather in the last three weeks had been favourable for the sugar beet crop.
"We've had cold, sunny weather in the past couple of weeks and that's been beneficial for sugar development," he said.
He said the sugar content should be at the high end of expectations at around 16.2 percent but maintained his overall Dutch production forecast at near one million tonnes.
In Belgium, latest test results showed a significant increase in sugar content compared with tests conducted at the start of September.

The Royal Belgian Institute for Improvement of Sugar Beet (IRAB) said an informal test on September 16 showed sugar contents were up to 15.5 percent. Belgium's third and last official test was on September 2.
The institute cited wet weather as the reason for the improvement in sugar contents and said more rain was forecast.
Sugar yields are expected to average 10 tonnes per hectare.
